frameworks.name: Cowen & Keltner 27 emotion categories (semantic space of reported experience)

citation.title: Self-report captures 27 distinct categories of emotion bridged by continuous gradients
citation.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 114(38), E7900-E7909

frameworks.summary: Using 2,185 short videos rated by 853 participants on 34 categories and 14 affective dimensions, finds that self-reported experience is organized into 27 distinct varieties bridged by continuous gradients, and that categories (e.g., amusement) explain reports better than valence/arousal. Unit of analysis: the reported emotional experience evoked by a stimulus, mapped as a high-dimensional semantic space.

constructs.label: 27 distinct emotion categories
constructs.notes: 26 of these are unambiguous in the paper. The paper is internally inconsistent on the 27th: the Results text excludes 'pride' ('pride and triumph, which coloaded on experiences of admiration'), whereas the Fig. 1 caption's exclusion list is '(contempt, disappointment, envy, guilt, relief, sympathy, and triumph)', which would exclude 'relief' and include 'pride'. This list follows the Results text (relief in, pride out), which also matches the authors' published interactive map. Flag for crosswalk: pride/relief ambiguity is in the primary source itself.

constructs.label: 34 categories rated (superset)
constructs.notes: 27 distinct + the 7 excluded categories named in the paper (contempt, disappointment, envy, guilt, sympathy, triumph, plus pride or relief depending on passage).

constructs.label: Continuous gradients between categories
constructs.notes: Categories are bridged by smooth gradients rather than discrete boundaries; the 14 affective-dimension scales (e.g., valence, arousal) were rated but found less explanatory than categories. The 14 scale names were not extracted.

frameworks.verification_notes: Bibliographic metadata and the category list verified from the PMC full text (pnas.org returned 403). The Results-vs-Fig.1 discrepancy on pride/relief was confirmed by direct quotation.

frameworks.name: SenticNet — Hourglass of Emotions (2012) and Hourglass Model Revisited (2020)

citation.authors: Cambria, Erik; Livingstone, Andrew; Hussain, Amir (2012); Susanto, Yosephine; Livingstone, Andrew G.; Ng, Bee Chin; Cambria, Erik (2020)
citation.title: The Hourglass of Emotions (LNCS 7403, pp. 144-157) / The Hourglass Model Revisited (IEEE Intelligent Systems 35(5):96-102)
citation.venue: Cognitive Behavioural Systems 2011, LNCS 7403, Springer 2012; IEEE Intelligent Systems, Sept/Oct 2020

frameworks.summary: The Hourglass of Emotions is SenticNet's emotion categorisation model: four independent but concomitant affective dimensions, each a float in [-1,+1] divided into six 'sentic levels' (three positive, three negative), from which compound emotions and a scalar polarity are derived. Units are lowercase emotion level names (e.g. joy, calmness) and dimension names; SenticNet concept entries carry a polarity label/value and Hourglass mood labels.
frameworks.identifier_scheme: Dimension name + sentic level label (lowercase), e.g. Introspection: joy; sentic vector = 4 floats in [-1,+1]; SenticNet entries use '#'-prefixed mood labels (e.g. #joy) with polarity_label positive|negative and polarity_value in [-1,1] (data-file schema from knowledge).

constructs.label: Hourglass of Emotions (2012) — four dimensions
constructs.notes: Each dimension is a float in [-1,+1]; level boundaries defined via a Gaussian G(x) at G(1), G(2/3), G(1/3), G(0), -G(1/3), -G(2/3), -G(1). Polarity p = sum over concepts of (Pleasantness + |Attention| - |Sensitivity| + Aptitude) / 3N.

constructs.label: Hourglass of Emotions (2012) — six sentic levels per dimension (Table 3), most positive to most negative
values: Pleasantness|ecstasy, joy, serenity, pensiveness, sadness, grief
Attention|vigilance, anticipation, interest, distraction, surprise, amazement
Sensitivity|rage, anger, annoyance, apprehension, fear, terror
Aptitude|admiration, trust, acceptance, boredom, disgust, loathing

constructs.label: Hourglass of Emotions (2012) — second-level (compound) emotions, Table 4
values: Pleasantness>0 x (Attention>0, Attention<0, Aptitude>0, Aptitude<0)|optimism, frivolity, love, gloat
Pleasantness<0 x (Attention>0, Attention<0, Aptitude>0, Aptitude<0)|frustration, disapproval, envy, remorse
Sensitivity>0 x (Attention>0, Attention<0, Aptitude>0, Aptitude<0)|aggressiveness, rejection, rivalry, contempt
Sensitivity<0 x (Attention>0, Attention<0, Aptitude>0, Aptitude<0)|anxiety, awe, submission, coercion
constructs.notes: Pairwise combination of sentic levels; e.g. love = joy (Pleasantness) + trust (Aptitude). Note awe = Sensitivity<0 x Attention<0 (fear + surprise); anxiety = Sensitivity<0 x Attention>0. Three/four-level compounds also allowed (e.g. joy + trust + anger = jealousy).

constructs.label: Hourglass Model Revisited (2020) — four dimensions
constructs.uri_or_code: Susanto et al. 2020, IEEE Intelligent Systems 35(5)
constructs.notes: Polarity formula (1): p_c = (I_c + T_c + A_c + S_c) / (|sgn(I_c)| + |sgn(T_c)| + |sgn(A_c)| + |sgn(S_c)|), i.e. sum of active dimension values divided by number of active dimensions; polarity in [-1,+1]. Surprise and other neutral emotions removed; calmness and eagerness added; antithetic emotions mirrored.

Table 1 (compound emotions, read from image) places: love/enjoyment/amusement = JOY+PLEASANTNESS; euphoria = JOY+EAGERNESS; enlightenment = JOY+CALMNESS; hate = SADNESS+DISGUST; distress = SADNESS+FEAR; envy = SADNESS+ANGER; hatred = ANGER+DISGUST; awe/submission/reverence = PLEASANTNESS+FEAR; kindness = PLEASANTNESS+EAGERNESS; hope/anticipation/optimism = EXPECTATION+JOY; hopelessness = EXPECTATION+SADNESS; shock = SURPRISE+ANGER; alarm = SURPRISE+FEAR; amazement/astonishment/wonderstruckness = SURPRISE+PLEASANTNESS.
